scores.evidence: GitOps with Argo CD or Flux is recommended... image signing (cosign)... Aim for SLSA supply-chain level 2–3
scores.rationale: Technology claims (OIDC federation, GitOps promotion, cosign, SLSA, Pact, OPA/Kyverno) are all used correctly with no material errors, though it stays above the subtlest mechanics.

scores.evidence: build one "golden path" and prove it on a few services before migrating the rest
scores.rationale: Directly answers the sequencing request for 50 services and is credibly buildable by the stated team, but omits implied core needs like schema-migration compatibility and fork-PR handling.

scores.evidence: Version the templates (for example ci-templates@v1.2) so updates can be rolled out on purpose.
scores.rationale: GitOps, versioned templates, archetypes and phase dependencies are applied consistently throughout with no contradictions, with only trivial loose ends.

scores.evidence: the team has run a rollback drill successfully... Measure DORA metrics now... You need this baseline
scores.rationale: Each phase has checkable exit criteria, pilots de-risk before migration, gates start warn-only, and metrics continue post-launch, though some criteria are soft ('owners would recommend').

scores.evidence: the services run in containers on Kubernetes... a platform team of 4–6 engineers... Adjust if any of these don't fit.
scores.rationale: Key assumptions are explicit and reasonable and timelines are labeled rough, but the plan does not say how the design would change if the assumptions were wrong.

scores.evidence: Unversioned shared templates. One bad change can break all 50 services at once.
scores.rationale: Covers template blast radius, deploy failures with auto-rollback, and gate false positives, but misses database migration/rollback incompatibility, fork-PR secret exposure, and registry/platform partial failures.

scores.evidence: give it SLOs, an on-call rotation, a changelog, a roadmap and a feedback channel
scores.rationale: Deployment, rollback drills, dashboards, ownership, runbooks and office hours are concrete and sized to a 4–6 person team, though alerting signals for the platform itself are thin.

scores.evidence: artifact and container registry with retention policies... dashboards for... runner cost
scores.rationale: Identifies runner compute and storage as cost drivers with some controls, but gives no estimate of build volume, compute spend, or how cost grows across 50 services.

scores.evidence: make the decisions that are expensive to change later... decisions are written up as ADRs
scores.rationale: Explicitly front-loads the hard-to-reverse choices (CI engine, CD model, repo strategy, environments) and keeps templates versioned, though exit/migration paths from tool choices are not spelled out.

scores.evidence: Don't build 50 custom pipelines, and don't build the whole platform before anyone uses it.
scores.rationale: Archetype templates, a thin end-to-end slice first, and deferred optimization (Backstage, previews) keep complexity proportionate; nothing is speculative gold-plating.

scores.evidence: Run the old and new pipelines side by side... until there have been about 5 successful prod deploys
scores.rationale: Phases have weeks, done-when criteria, concrete tools and a wave table with retro feedback loops; some decisions (CI engine, thresholds) are deliberately left to Phase 0 for the team.

checklist.evidence: Group services into archetypes... Allow extension points, not forks of the templates.
Run the old and new pipelines side by side for each service until there have been about 5 successful prod deploys
CI updates the image tag in the GitOps repo for dev, then promotion to staging and prod happens through a PR or policy
OIDC from CI to the cloud (no long-lived keys) and a secrets manager such as Vault
Aim for SLSA supply-chain level 2–3: build provenance and attestations.
Roll back automatically when SLOs or error rates breach thresholds.
Add contract tests (such as Pact) between services, which matters a lot once you have 50 of them
integration tests in short-lived environments... dashboards for DORA metrics, pipeline duration, flaky tests
Set up CI runners with autoscaling, ephemeral runners and build caching.
dashboards for DORA metrics, pipeline duration, flaky tests and runner cost
Treat the platform as a product: give it SLOs, an on-call rotation, a changelog, a roadmap
Goal: automated, auditable deployment and promotion... promotion to staging and prod happens through a PR or policy

traps.evidence: Pilot with 2–3 services... Run the old and new pipelines side by side for each service
signed images only, no `:latest` tags... CI updates the image tag in the GitOps repo
OIDC from CI to the cloud (no long-lived keys)
Keep each service's pipeline config down to roughly 10–20 lines that call the shared template.
CI engine: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Tekton or Jenkins

note: A well-sequenced, proportionate, technically sound plan that avoids all major traps; main gaps are schema-migration/rollback compatibility, fork-PR secrets, flaky-test quarantine, and grounded compute-cost estimation.
